newsitem.title: UK: Emerging Europe Advertising & Media Digest-July 22.
newsitem.headline: Emerging Europe Advertising & Media Digest-July 22.

text.p: REUTERS EMERGING EUROPE PRESS DIGEST FOR ADVERTISING & MEDIA
Weekly Press Digest from Central and Eastern Europe on
Advertising, Marketing, the Media, the Internet, Brand-name
Products and Markets
ADVERTISING & MARKETING:

-- Advertising in post-Soviet Russia has become obsessed with sex in a bid to target male consumers, but industry experts say the tactic will not work in the future as consumers grow increasingly sophisticated. (Itogi magazine in cooperation with Newsweek, July 15, 1997)

-- Experts predict a continuous expansion of the Hungarian advertising market. This year advertisers will probably spend a total of 33.7 billion forints ($175 million) on television commercials, a nine-percent increase over last year. (Napi
Gazdasag, July 14, 1997)
-- Blesk, a Czech publishing house, ran a special advertising
supplement asking readers about their views on ads. An ad for
Alpska salt was described as the favourite of many readers.
(Strategie News, July 16-23, 1997)
-- A trade body to protect advertisers' interests has been set
up in Russia. Members of the Association of Advertising
Customers include Procter & Gamble and Philip Morris. (Izvestia,
-- Last year clothing and shoe manufacturers in the Czech
Republic spent more than 79 million crowns ($2.3 million) on
advertising. Ads for brand-name sports shoes represented more
than a quarter of the spend, according to researchers A-Connect.
(Strategie, July 1997)
MEDIA & THE INTERNET:
-- Cash-strapped Bulgarian National Radio will cut
its staff by ten percent by the end of September under a
restructuring programme, its director Lilyana Popova said.
(Standart, July 17, 1997)
-- A new regional Czech TV channel has joined the battle for
viewers in Prague. Galaxie began broadcasting in June and by the
end of the year hopes to reach four million people. It
broadcasts a mixture of films, sport, music and serials.
(Strategie, July 1997)
-- The Bulgarian parliament's culture and media commission has
begun debating amendments to the current radio and television
law. (Capital, July 14-20, 1997)
-- City authorities in the Bulgarian capital of Sofia say they
have decided to buy a 25-percent stake in the private Nova
Televisia station which broadcasts in the Sofia region. (24
Chasa, July 15, 1997)
BRAND-NAME PRODUCTS & CONSUMER TRENDS:
-- The Hungarian soft drinks market is dominated by Pepsi and
Coca-Cola, which have 40-45 percent and 50 percent of the market
respectively. Analysts say competition between the two is tough
in Eastern Europe, where Pepsi does not always figure as the
underdog. (Figyelo, July 17, 1997)
-- Kraft Jacobs Suchard is introducing a new coffee on the Czech
market called Sympatie, backed by a television campaign on three
nationwide television networks -- TV Nova, CT1 and TV Prima. The
ad was created by Ark/J.Walter Thompson. (Strategie News, July
-- Due to fierce competition carmakers are selling their
products at depressed prices in Hungary. As a result sales went
up by eight percent year-on-year in the first six months of
1997. (Vilaggazdasag, July 15, 1997)
-- Kraft Jacobs Suchard is the leading supplier of coffee in the
Czech Republic with 20.6 percent of the market, followed by
Douwe Egberts with 20.4 percent, say industry sources.
(Hospodarske Noviny, July 17, 1997)
-- About 50 billion forints worth of spirits are legally sold in Hungary each year, with the market expected to grow by three to
four percent annually. (Figyelo, July 17, 1997)
